title: Dispatch TUR 9: Westmere Survivors Begin Life Before Their Birth
summary: The inquiry closes the station and keeps the warnings that brought the train home.
author: Clara Vale, Staff Correspondent
paragraphs: The temporary platform has been dismantled, the council announced yesterday. Its clock, lamps, and name board remain together in the Eidetical Institute. Dr. Saye says keeping the pieces may allow a controlled study of the passage without leaving a station open in a public yard.

The 106 passengers are housed with relatives or in municipal lodgings. Their records retain their own dates of birth and the date on which they arrived here. Officials have declined to invent earlier birthdays to make the registers appear orderly. Guard Pell, whose parents are still living in Kingsfen, has chosen not to visit them yet.

Mrs. Harrow says Miriam has begun asking which of her school friends have been born. She has put the child’s drawings beside the kitchen clock. “I told her I cannot promise to know everything that will happen,” Mrs. Harrow said. “I can promise she has a place to come home to.”

Dr. Saye has submitted the letters warning of the marsh flood to the council for preservation and planning. There are twelve years in which to survey the district, she said, though she cautions that altering the future may alter the route by which its warning arrived.

Mr. Pike closed his inquiry with a narrower conclusion. Every Westmere letter delivered by his office had an address, a sender, and a journey. “That is all a postman requires,” he said. At the abandoned bridge pier this morning, fresh coal grit lay above the marsh line. No rails led to it.
